summary:
Tierra del Fuego, an Argentine province, stands under Argentina's national framework, which remains among the most permissive in the world for legal gender recognition. Law 26.743, promulgated on 24 May 2012 after passing the Chamber of Deputies 167-17-7 and the Senate 55 votes to one abstention on 9 May, allows a change of legal gender without surgery, hormone treatment or judicial approval, and it remains on the books. The United Nations described it as a pioneering step for transgender rights in the region. A trans adult visitor's identity documents are therefore not gated by medical approval on arrival.

The framework has been narrowed by executive action. On 5 February 2025 the government of President Javier Milei issued a decree restricting minors' access to gender-affirming surgery and hormone treatment, reported by Reuters as a ban on those procedures for adolescents; a second decree governs the housing of transgender people in prisons. Legal experts interviewed by Agencia Presentes called the measure illegal and unconstitutional and signalled an intention to seek judicial intervention, so its litigation status is unresolved. The same government eliminated the federal Women, Gender and Diversity Ministry and dismissed trans employees hired under the Trans Labour Quota Law.

Practical exposure to violence is the operative visitor concern. The Observatorio Nacional de Crímenes de Odio recorded at least 227 hate crimes based on sexual orientation or gender identity across 2025, a record, averaging one every 38 hours and up on 2024. Trans women and travestis accounted for 62.5% of victims (142 people), with 18 trans men targeted against 5 in 2024, alongside 13 lesbians and 4 non-binary people. Physical violence made up 64.8% of cases (147).

Police contact is where the exposure concentrates. About 32% of the 2025 cases occurred inside police stations or penal institutions, and recorded police involvement rose from 17 cases in 2024 to 64 in 2025. For a traveler, that is the authorities-contact surface met on any stop, search or detention rather than a background risk.

Argentine trans activists interviewed on 4 April 2025, including representatives of organisations named for Diana Sacayán, killed in 2015, and for the activist Lohana Berkins, described the community as facing a chaotic and desperate situation with heightened exposure to violence, discrimination and poverty under the Milei government's policies.

No Tierra del Fuego-specific deviation from the national position has been sourced material enough to score separately, so the province is assessed at the national score.
tangentialFactors:
Argentina was the first Latin American country to legalise marriage equality, in 2010, and anti-discrimination protection exists through a combination of national and provincial laws, giving a trans visitor a wider statutory shield than the enforcement record suggests.

Outright International's country overview, updated in March 2026, records negative assessments for same-sex relations, gender recognition and the registration of civil-society organisations, and assesses deterioration against the earlier statutory position.

The judicial response to gender-motivated killing is contested. In April 2025 Argentina's Supreme Court left standing the life sentence imposed on Gabriel Marino for the 2015 murder of trans activist Diana Sacayán while rejecting attempts to reinstate the travesticidio aggravating circumstance that an appeals court removed in 2020, so the gender-motivated aggravation is not currently applied in that line of cases.
localsOnly:
Residents retain a route to legal gender change without surgery, hormone treatment or judicial approval under Law 26.743, and that statutory text has not been repealed.

The Trans Labour Quota Law reserved at least 1% of public-sector jobs for trans people; trans employees hired under it were dismissed by the Milei government, and the federal Women, Gender and Diversity Ministry was eliminated, removing the state body that had administered those measures.

Residents who are minors are affected by the 5 February 2025 decree restricting access to gender-affirming surgery and hormone treatment, a measure legal experts called unconstitutional and signalled an intention to challenge in court.

Transgender residents held in custody are governed by a separate decree on prison housing issued in February 2025, which bears directly on where a trans detainee is placed.
outOfScopeNotes:
No Tierra del Fuego-specific source on provincial police practice, provincial prison placement of transgender detainees, or provincial implementing rules was available in this inventory; the province is described here purely through the national framework, and whether Tierra del Fuego's own police or correctional authorities depart from national practice is unresolved and not sourced.

The current litigation status of the February 2025 decrees is unresolved: sources record the intention of legal experts to seek judicial intervention but do not report a ruling, so whether the decrees have been stayed or upheld is not sourced.

Facilities-side questions, including availability of gender-affirming care for visitors in Tierra del Fuego and local hate-crime reporting channels, are not sourced in this inventory and remain unverified.
